record.title: Exploring human–AI collaboration for management control in public healthcare

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: International Journal of Public Sector Management
record.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how controllers in public healthcare envision human–AI collaboration in management control when dealing with uncertainty, complexity and equivocality, focusing on anticipated advantages and implementation challenges in an early-adoption setting. Design/methodology/approach We conducted an exploratory qualitative study with 14 controllers from Italian public healthcare organisations. Four closed-ended questions provided a preliminary picture of current AI adoption, while three scenario-based open-ended questions elicited prospective assessments. The framework method was used to analyse the data. Findings AI adoption remains limited and uneven, and is rarely embedded in everyday management control. Under uncertainty, controllers link AI to better forecasting and faster access to information, but worry about data quality, privacy and overreliance. In complex settings, they expect AI to help integrate diverse information and enable more systemic control, provided processes are standardised and human oversight remains. In equivocal situations, AI may support interpretation and communication, but its impact is limited by limited hands-on experience and the difficulty of codifying contextual nuances. Originality/value Based on the Jarrahi (2018) decision-making scenarios, the study develops a tentative conceptualisation of how public healthcare controllers envisage AI collaboration. The concerns of the participants inform three proposed arrangements: validation, recursive integration and contestable sensemaking. Their formulation and the accountability-augmentation principle are theoretical elaborations informed by prospective evidence and accountability research.

record.abstract_text: Purpose Agentic AI systems execute procurement decisions, reroute shipments and renegotiate supplier contracts at speeds that preclude real-time human review. The existing literature offers limited analytical attention to the risks that arise when decision authority is delegated to agents. This paper develops a risk taxonomy for agentic AI in supply chains and traces the hierarchical dependencies and influence magnitudes among the identified risks. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of literature, analyzed through theories–characteristics–contexts–methods framework, produces the risk taxonomy. A hybrid modified total interpretive structural modeling and fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory methodology is then applied to structured expert judgments to establish the causal hierarchy and quantify inter-risk influence. Findings Three risks, namely workforce skill gap, data quality and reliability and ethical misalignment occupy the deepest level of the causal hierarchy. Lack of accountability and governance and data privacy emerge as terminal outcomes. All three analytical methods converge on a conclusion: agentic AI risks originate at the institutional layer, with technical risks acting as transmission mechanisms. Practical implications The findings indicate that effective governance requires that workforce capability, data integrity and objective-function alignment are addressed before deployment. The stratified agentic AI governance framework is proposed that translates hierarchical structure into a sequenced intervention architecture, providing practitioners with governance priorities organized by risk-propagation logic. Originality/value This paper contributes a systematically derived risk taxonomy and a causally weighted governance map for agentic AI risks in supply chains. Five propositions are derived from the causal structure and are advanced as a testable research agenda.

record.abstract_text: Purpose As artificial intelligence advances and its application scenarios continue to expand, human–artificial intelligence interaction grows increasingly close. While artificial intelligence brings convenience, it also raises concerns that it may weaken users' cognitive autonomy. To investigate this issue. This study aims to explore the composition of AI dependence and its impact on cognitive autonomy and specific aspects of creative performance. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on cognitive evaluation theory and the elaboration likelihood model to construct a dual-pathway model with instrumental dependence and affective dependence as core variables. The model explains the formation mechanisms of the two types of artificial intelligence dependence and their differential effects on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily examines their potential role in the elaboration dimension of creative performance. A two-stage mixed-method design was employed to test the model. Findings Study 1 found that perceived trust mainly had a positive effect on instrumental dependence. Different dimensions of interactivity differentially affected affective dependence and cognitive autonomy. Mediation analysis further confirmed the core mediating role of Dependence. Study 2, a small-sample exploratory experiment, re-tested selected hypotheses and found a possible negative effect of instrumental dependence on the elaboration dimension of creative performance. Research limitations/implications The main theoretical contribution of this study lies in revealing the dual-pathway formation mechanisms of artificial intelligence dependence and the reshaping effects of different types of dependence on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily explores the potential effects of dependence on elaboration performance. Originality/value The dual-pathway dependence model constructed in this study offers practical implications for understanding how long-term use of artificial intelligence affects cognitive autonomy.

record.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how knowledge workers make sense of GenAI-enabled co-production, with particular attention to authorship ambiguity and its implications for competence attribution, self-evaluation and meaningful work. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative approach based on in-depth interviews with 32 knowledge workers who work directly with GenAI tools, combining inductive coding with abductive interpretation. We used the Gioia methodology to analyze participants' reported experiences and interpretations of human–AI collaboration, with sensemaking informing the interpretation of emergent themes and aggregate dimensions. Findings The findings identify authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. When GenAI contributes to ideation, analysis, drafting, coding or other knowledge-intensive outputs, workers may find it difficult to distinguish their own contribution from that of the technology. Participants responded to this ambiguity differently. Some reconstructed their expertise around judgment, validation and contextualization and experienced GenAI as extending their professional capability. Others struggled to internalize successful outputs as evidence of their own competence and reported impostor-like experiences and reduced meaningfulness. The findings suggest that experiences of GenAI-enabled co-production depend on whether workers interpret and reconstruct their contribution. Practical implications Managers in comparable knowledge-intensive settings may consider making human judgment visible, clarifying legitimate uses of GenAI and recognizing contributions beyond output speed and quality. Originality/value This study identifies authorship ambiguity as a central interpretive challenge in GenAI-mediated knowledge work. It shows how uncertainty regarding the respective contributions of the worker and GenAI can complicate competence attribution and initiate sensemaking about professional contribution. By explaining how workers' interpretations of authorship ambiguity are associated with divergent identity and meaning outcomes, including enhanced capability, impostor-like experiences and changing meaningfulness, the study extends research on human–AI collaboration beyond its predominant focus on performance and productivity.

record.title: Algorithmic cognitive programmes: observing ambient architectures of attention with social systems theory

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Purpose This paper extends Luhmann's concept of programmes – decision premises specifying the conditions under which a system's binary code is operatively assigned – into the domain of algorithmically mediated communication. It conceptualises recommendation systems, ranking algorithms and feedback architectures as ambient cognitive programmes: recursive, probabilistic selectors that perturb the structural coupling between social and psychic systems, and examines the constitutional implications of their opacity and transfunctional reach. Design/methodology/approach The study develops a systemic–cybernetic model grounded in Luhmann's social systems theory and the epistemology of autopoietic cognition, integrating Teubner's theory of societal constitutionalism to address the normative dimensions of algorithmic mediation. Analytical illustrations from Facebook and TikTok contrast two recommendation architectures – affinity-based cascading and behavioural-similarity propagation – to demonstrate how the model applies across distinct platform logics. Findings Algorithmic cognitive programmes operate as meta-programmes that reconfigure multiple forms of social differentiation simultaneously, enacting a binary operational distinction of visibility/invisibility through engagement metrics. Their colonisation of communicative environments – by economic imperatives and, as the analysis argues, by the autonomous logic of technical mediation – becomes a constitutional pathology where its effects cannot be contested or corrected, requiring internal self-limiting mechanisms that render operative selection criteria observable to affected systems. Originality/value The paper advances a novel theoretical category – ambient cognitive programmes – that extends Luhmann's organisational typology by identifying a configuration it does not explicitly address: a purpose programme without a terminal goal state that continuously revises the conditional programmes it governs. It connects this analytical framework to Teubner's societal constitutionalism, proposing constitutional observability as a structural condition for the compatibility between algorithmic regimes and communicative pluralism.

record.title: From Learner Modeling to Human–AI Co-Regulation: A Systematic Scoping Review of Adaptive Generative AI in Personalized Learning

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

record.title: AI Anxiety, Digital Overload, and Technostress in a Polycrisis Context: A Moderated Mediation Study of Emotional Exhaustion and Psychological Well-Being Across Four Industry Sectors

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background : The concurrent occurrence of AI-induced disruption, rapid post-pandemic digitalization, and macroeconomic instability has fundamentally reshaped the psychological demands of modern work, creating a polycrisis. Staff members in digital work environments experience rising AI anxiety, digital overload, and technostress, but how such polycrisis-related demands impact PWB through these mechanisms and the extent to which personal resources may act as a shield against such an effect has not been comprehensively understood yet. Based on the assumptions of the Job Demands-Resources model, the present study examines a model of moderated mediation, wherein emotional exhaustion mediates the demand-PWB association, and psychological capital (PsyCap) moderates and strengthens PWB. Methods: Cross-sectional surveys using six psychometric scales were conducted among 340 full-time workers from sectors such as IT, Health care, Education, and Banking/Finance. Hypotheses regarding the structure were validated using CB-SEM with 5,000 bias corrected bootstraps whereas sector-specific MGA and fsQCA identified configurations related to lower PWB. Results: All three job demands were able to predict emotional exhaustion: AI anxiety (β = 0.396, p < 0.001), digital overload (β = 0.333, p < 0.001), and technostress (β = 0.318, p < 0.001), explaining 32.1% of the variance. Emotional exhaustion fully mediated the influence of all three variables on PWB (β = -0.434, p < 0.001) through bootstrapped indirect effects. PsyCap had a significant direct effect on PWB (β = 0.460, p < 0.001) for all four sectors. Through MGA, sector-specific differences emerged with regard to AI anxiety, which was more important in the IT sector, digital overload in Healthcare and Banking/Finance, and technostress in the Education sector. In fsQCA, digital overload was found as a necessary condition for low PWB (consistency = 0.909), where there were three configurations, each required low PsyCap as a boundary condition (solution consistency = 0.841, coverage = 0.573). Conclusions: Demands resulting from polycrisis are linked to low PWB mainly because of emotional exhaustion, and demand salience differs significantly across sectors. Low PsyCap functions as a universal boundary condition for low levels of well-being. Organisations should prioritise PsyCap development as an industry-invariant approach in addition to demand management, which takes into account the characteristics of the job.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background Natural language processing and AI models are increasingly used to extract emotional signals from textual data; however, systematic validation of different computational paradigms in emotionally complex relational contexts remains limited. Such approaches may contribute to digital health research, particularly in the fields of digital mental health and couples therapy, where understanding emotional expressions within romantic relationships is especially relevant. Objective This study aimed to compare a lexicon-based approach (NRC Emotion Lexicon) and a transformer-based model (Pysentimiento) in detecting affective patterns within spontaneous romantic relationship narratives and to evaluate their criterion-related associations with a theory-driven measure of relational well-being. Methods In this cross-sectional exploratory study, 112 Spanish adults completed the Couple Flourishing Measure (CFM) and provided an open-ended description of their romantic relationship. Narratives were analyzed using both computational approaches to generate emotion and sentiment indices. Pearson correlations were computed between model outputs and CFM scores. Steiger Z tests were conducted to compare dependent correlations across models. Results Both approaches showed significant associations with couple flourishing, although the transformer-based model yielded stronger correlations for several affective dimensions, particularly positive sentiment ( r =0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.76) and negative sentiment ( r =−0.74, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.65). The lexicon-based approach showed smaller associations, primarily for negative emotions. Steiger Z tests identified significant between-model differences for disgust ( P =.04), joy ( P =.01), sadness ( P =.004), surprise ( P =.03), and positive and negative sentiment (both P <.001), but not for anger or fear. Conclusions In this sample, Pysentimiento showed stronger associations with couple flourishing than the NRC Emotion Lexicon across several affective dimensions, although differences were not consistent across all categories. These findings support the value of theory-driven external criteria for evaluating computational emotion detection in relational narratives and underscore the importance of context-sensitive interpretation when applying AI tools in psychologically sensitive domains. These findings also highlight the potential relevance of computational emotion analysis for digital health research, particularly in digital mental health and couples therapy research, although further validation in clinical settings is needed before clinical implementation.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Background AI is increasingly embedded in health care and digital health applications, shaping clinical processes as well as how patients access information and participate in care. Research on bias in medical AI has largely focused on technical and performance-related disparities. Less attention has been paid to how such biases may affect patients’ access, understanding, trust, and opportunities for meaningful involvement in care. Objective This scoping review aimed to map how studies of bias in medical AI describe patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment and the digital divide and to identify gaps across technical, social, structural, and patient-centered perspectives. Methods This scoping review followed JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute) methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE and EBSCOHost databases were searched in August 2025 and supplemented by Google Scholar searches. Peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 onward were included if they addressed bias in medical AI and described patient-related consequences relevant to patient empowerment or digital inequality. Data charting focused on AI application types, bias dimensions, patient empowerment domains, digital divide–related factors, intersectionality, and debiasing strategies. Findings were synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results The search identified 497 records, of which 22 studies met the inclusion criteria. Bias was represented as a multidimensional sociotechnical phenomenon, with social bias identified most frequently (21/22 studies), followed by algorithmic bias (16/22 studies), structural bias (14/22 studies), and design-related bias (12/22 studies). Patient empowerment was most frequently addressed through involvement in care (n=13), followed by health literacy (n=9) and trust and assurance (n=7), whereas broader psychosocial and everyday-life domains were addressed less frequently. Digital divide–related factors were identified in 19 of the 22 studies, with digital literacy and usability barriers reported most frequently. Seven studies considered 2 or more social or structural dimensions of disadvantage. Although many studies discussed approaches that could mitigate bias-related barriers, explicit empirical evaluation of debiasing strategies in relation to patient empowerment or digital equity was largely absent. Conclusions Patient-related consequences of bias in medical AI extend beyond algorithmic performance and are reflected in access, understanding, trust, and involvement in care. Broader empowerment dimensions, multidimensional disadvantage, and empirically evaluated mitigation strategies remain comparatively underexplored.

record.title: Characterizing University Students’ Geometric Thinking Through Dialogues with Generative Artificial Intelligence in Geometry Transformation Learning

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a promising technology for supporting mathematical dialogue, feedback, and reasoning in mathematics education. However, research has paid limited attention to how university students’ geometric thinking develops through sustained interaction with GenAI, particularly in geometry transformation learning. This study aims to develop a Dialogic Geometric Thinking Framework that characterizes the dimensions and progression of university students’ geometric thinking during sustained dialogue with ChatGPT. A qualitative exploratory design was employed involving undergraduate mathematics education students enrolled in a Geometry Transformation course at an Indonesian public university. Data were collected from student–ChatGPT dialogue transcripts, students’ written solutions, and reflective interviews. The data were analyzed thematically using reflexive thematic analysis to identify recurring characteristics and relationships among dimensions of geometric thinking and to synthesize them into an integrated framework. The findings identified five interrelated dimensions of geometric thinking: conceptual reasoning, representational coordination, procedural justification, reflective regulation, and mathematical elaboration. These dimensions illustrate how students progressively articulate mathematical concepts, coordinate representations, justify solution procedures, evaluate their reasoning, and extend mathematical ideas during AI-mediated dialogue. The study resulted in a Dialogic Geometric Thinking Framework that provides a process-oriented perspective on the development of university students’ geometric thinking during interaction with GenAI. The framework offers an initial theoretical foundation for understanding and further investigating geometric thinking in AI-mediated mathematics learning. Keywords: geometric thinking, generative artificial intelligence, chatGPT, geometry transformation, mathematical dialogue.

record.title: A Teacher's Concerns about AI in Primary School: Critical Thinking, Personal Data and the Fear of Cognitive Dependence

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. Written from the perspective of a primary school teacher and principal, this perspective paper examines three interrelated concerns of the author herself. These concerns arose from a wish to protect her pupils and led her to study the topic for her own professional development and to help her colleagues make teaching safer and better. They concern developing critical thinking towards AI-generated answers, protecting the personal data of minors, and the fear that excessive assistance from AI will weaken pupils' thinking. Drawing on a narrative, non-systematic review of recent research on cognitive offloading, the European and Greek regulatory framework, and illustrative examples from the author's own teaching practice and lesson scenarios for primary school, it argues that the fear of cognitive dependence is a plausible concern rather than an established finding for primary school pupils. The available evidence, which comes mainly from adolescents and adults, suggests that the form of AI support (whether it replaces the learner's effort or scaffolds it) may be an important factor. AI is regarded throughout as a valuable tool; the risk lies mainly in the way it is used. The classroom examples come from ordinary lessons whose only purpose was to teach pupils to question AI answers and to protect themselves when using AI. They were not planned as research, no research data were collected, and they are offered as the author's practitioner reflections, not as findings. The author's classroom experience illustrates that such activities can be implemented in ordinary primary school lessons, but their effects on pupils' critical thinking have not yet been evaluated. The paper relates the three concerns to long-standing educational principles, in particular Socratic questioning, Dewey's reflective thought and Vygotskian scaffolding. On this basis, it proposes a simple, as yet untested three-step classroom protocol (``think -- ask -- check''), age-appropriate data protection rules, and a role for school leadership, and outlines questions for future research.

record.title: Minds Meet Machines: The Joint Role of Trust and Intellectual Humility in AI Persuasion

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Research shows that AI models have a remarkable ability to change people’s minds following a short conversation, a notoriously difficult task for human communicators. Such persuasive paradigms provide a unique opportunity to examine which psychological characteristics predict receptivity to counter-attitudinal information. We focus on two characteristics: intellectual humility (IH), reflecting openness to revising one’s beliefs following new information, and trust in the information source (AI). To establish the role of a-priori dispositions that determine acceptance of new information, we ran two online studies, sampling British participants with a negative attitude toward legal immigrants (N = 294). We replicated previous findings showing significant and lasting attitude change following a brief exchange with GPT, but crucially, this effect was not uniform. In Study 1, attitude change was greatest among participants with higher initial trust in AIs and higher intellectual humility. Study 2 extended this finding by measuring both dispositions a week before the conversation with GPT, revealing the same pattern: opinion change was greatest among those who were both open to new information and trusting of its source. These findings highlight the centrality of recipient dispositions, suggesting that the relationship between source trust and persuasion depends on recipients' intellectual humility. More broadly, source trust may function as more than a heuristic cue, and its relationship with attitude change may depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the fallibility of their beliefs. Together, these findings extend perspectives on persuasion by highlighting the joint role of source trust and recipients' epistemic dispositions in belief revision.

record.title: CardioTwin-AI: development and internal validation of a digital twin-based adaptive risk-aware learning framework for heart disease prediction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Heart disease is one of the most common causes of death in the world and early identification of individuals at elevated cardiovascular risk requires reliable risk-assessment methods that can support clinical decision-making. Many conventional machine-learning models focus primarily on disease classification or risk prediction and do not explicitly provide patient-specific virtual representations. This study introduces CardioTwin-AI, a Digital Twin-based Adaptive Risk-Aware Learning Framework (ARLF) to predict the presence or absence of heart disease. We propose a data-driven, patient-specific Digital Twin representation based on clinical attributes, in which the patient state is mapped to a corresponding virtual state and evaluated using state-level synchronization measures, including Twin Simulation Error (TSE) and Twin Fidelity Score (TFS) to quantify representation consistency. The deep feature representations are generated by feature engineering process based on autoencoder, and then analysed by the ARLF prediction model to estimate the probability of the presence of heart disease. It achieved high patient-state representation consistency between the source clinical state and its virtual representation, with a Twin Fidelity Score of 99.76% and a Twin Simulation Error of 0.002402. The proposed ARLF model achieved accuracy of 90.21%, precision of 90.32%, recall of 94.11%, F1-score of 92.18%, and ROC-AUC of 95.13% in the fixed held-out evaluation. The results indicate the potential of CardioTwin-AI for predicting the presence or absence of heart disease and assessing patient-state representation consistency, subject to further external validation and prospective clinical evaluation.

record.abstract_text: Introduction Watershed environmental governance increasingly combines dense sensing infrastructure with institutions whose attention, authority, and coordination capacity remain limited. We develop the cognitive orchestration layer as a theory-building concept for examining how large language model (LLM)-based agents may connect sensing, assessment, decision advice, institutional response, and feedback without displacing domain models or public authority. Methods The Agentic Framework for Watershed Governance (AFWG) specifies three enabling pathways, three institutional interfaces, and four propositions. A purposively selected set of eight publicly documented cases is used to illustrate functional configurations, source limitations, and research gaps; it is not a systematic review or empirical evaluation. Results The cases document sensing, assessment, and decision-support functions, but do not establish improved decision quality, sustained institutional use, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO is retained as an adjacent-domain design illustration, not an existence proof of full-loop closure: human authorization remains necessary, and its reported performance has not been independently replicated. Discussion Transfer to watershed governance is plausible only where domain models remain authoritative, outputs carry provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain authority to authorize consequential actions, and institutional audit and failure handling are built into deployment. AFWG therefore offers a bounded conceptual framework and a falsifiable research agenda, rather than a claim that agents have already closed the watershed response loop.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Introduction Artificial intelligence is transforming higher education and professional communication, creating a tension between technological automation and human critical thinking. In teaching communication, this tension highlights the need to rethink the skills students should develop as AI becomes increasingly integrated into academic and professional practice, especially the ability to use AI strategically without losing human judgment, ethical reasoning, and decision-making in their context. Methodology The study uses an exploratory-descriptive, cross-sectional, mixed-methods design combining quantitative and qualitative evidence to explore how students and program directors in Ecuador perceive AI integration in communication education. It surveyed 230 students across seven institutions and conducted 12 semi-structured interviews with directors. Survey analysis identified AI usage patterns, while thematic analysis of interviews focused on benefits, barriers, ethics, and priorities. Initially, Pearson's chi-square test examined associations with sociodemographics, but it was unreliable due to low expected cell counts. Findings are presented as descriptive patterns, not inferential or population-level conclusions. Results Students report using AI mainly for communication (28.70%), trend prediction and audience analysis (13.04%), and segmentation (9.57%). Four AI applications were identified: operational efficiency, strategic analysis, audience management, and digital optimization. The gender-based chi-square test was inconclusive ( χ 2 = 12.728; df = 14; p = 0.548), with over 50% of cells having fewer than 5 responses. Among directors and coordinators, common uses included content generation, assisted writing, research, data analysis, and audience engagement. The thematic analysis revealed four patterns: operational efficiency, decision-making, automation vs. human judgment, and training needs. Discussion and conclusions Communication students in Ecuador mainly use AI to improve efficiency and effectiveness, with key applications in trend prediction, audience analysis, and segmentation. Program leaders see AI as useful in content creation, research, and audience engagement. The study identifies four AI use areas: operational efficiency, strategic analysis, audience management, and digital optimization. The study highlights tension between automation and human judgment, stressing the continued importance of critical thinking, creativity, ethics, and context. It proposes a framework balancing AI automation with human input to support strategic communication decisions.

record.abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of online educational technologies, instructional videos have become a pivotal tool for flexible and efficient learning. The integration of visual aids, such as animations and dynamic elements, aims to enhance the learning experience; however, their effectiveness remains debated. This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static AI-generated images or manually animated versions of those images. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 undergraduate participants ( n = 10 per cell), comparing static versus motion-enhanced presentation conditions across male and female participant groups. Stable Diffusion XL generated the base images, and CapCut was used to add motion; the motion itself was not AI-generated. Participants viewed a 140-s mobile video on mortise-and-tenon structures, completed a 10-item accuracy test, and rated willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and mental effort. The ANOVA results provided no statistically significant evidence of a main effect of motion on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several subjective outcomes. For acceptability, the gender × motion interaction was statistically significant, but Bonferroni-adjusted simple-effect tests supported a gender-group difference only in the static condition. For mental effort, the interaction was also statistically significant; adjusted simple-effect tests indicated higher mental effort among female than male participants in the dynamic condition and higher mental effort in the static than dynamic condition among male participants. Given the small sample and multiple outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Background AI feedback holds promise for supporting student learning, but unstructured use can lead students to passively accept AI-generated answers, weakening their independent reasoning. This study examined whether structured AI feedback affects undergraduate students' critical thinking, learning performance, and engagement in a data science analytics course. Methods An exploratory two-class quasi-experimental study was conducted in a three-month undergraduate data science course ( N = 167). One class received four-phase structured AI feedback, while the comparison class received conventional instructor feedback. Propensity score matching was used to improve comparability on observed baseline characteristics. Critical thinking was assessed using an adapted 40-item assessment covering five dimensions. Results Students receiving structured AI feedback demonstrated higher post-test critical thinking scores than matched controls, with a baseline-adjusted difference of 5.64 points (95% CI [3.62, 7.65], p &lt; 0.001). A significant between-group difference in pre-to-post changes was also observed. Dimension-level analyses revealed significant differences in Evaluation of Arguments, Interpretation, Recognition of Assumptions, and Inference, while Deduction showed no significant difference. Higher learning performance, cognitive engagement, and behavioral engagement were also observed in the structured AI feedback group, whereas emotional engagement did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusion The findings provide exploratory evidence of differences in critical thinking and learning outcomes between the structured AI feedback and conventional instructor feedback classes. They highlight the potential relevance of feedback designs that encourage students to actively evaluate, question, and revise AI-supported analytical work, while underscoring the need for further studies that can isolate intervention-specific effects.

record.abstract_text: Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to obtain feedback in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing, but its educational significance depends on how learners interpret and regulate that feedback. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and self-regulated learning theory, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined an AI-supported motivated self-regulated learning framework using a cross-sectional survey of 486 university EFL students and follow-up interviews with 20 students. Structural equation modeling identified a positive direct association between reported AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement, together with a positive indirect statistical association through learning autonomy and self-regulated learning. The AI feedback use–autonomy association was stronger at higher modeled levels of AI literacy. Interview accounts described feedback-related control, critical evaluation, and awareness of AI limitations, alongside contrasting experiences of rapid polishing and careful evaluation despite limited familiarity with AI. Integration of the two strands highlighted variation in how learners evaluated and incorporated feedback. These self-report findings do not establish temporal ordering or causal effects. They identify learner agency, strategic regulation, and critical evaluation as relevant considerations for future investigations of AI-supported writing.

record.title: Information overload, cognitive fatigue, and postgraduates’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence for English academic writing: the role of lower-order cognitive offloading

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

record.title: From disclosure to epistemic accountability: preserving meaningful human control across the AI-assisted research lifecycle

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics
record.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded across the scientific research lifecycle, while prevailing governance remains centered on disclosure of tool use and the assignment of responsibility to human authors. We argue that disclosure is necessary but insufficient because it does not establish that researchers understood, verified, challenged, and authorized the AI-assisted processes that shaped scientific claims. We define this disconnect as the epistemic accountability gap and develop the Lifecycle Epistemic Accountability Framework (LEAF) as a testable theory of how meaningful human control can be preserved across AI-assisted knowledge production. Drawing on a structured integrative review and critical interpretive synthesis, LEAF links four human-control capacities—competence, contestability, intervention authority, and traceable ownership—supported by evaluability by design, to five lifecycle checkpoints spanning evidence identification, study design and ethics, data processing and analysis, interpretation, and reporting or knowledge translation. The framework proposes that accountability improves when oversight is exercised prospectively at epistemically consequential decision points, documented through an audit trail, and calibrated to epistemic materiality: the extent to which AI assistance can alter the validity, interpretation, or consequences of a scientific claim. Six propositions specify testable relationships among disclosure, epistemic materiality, meaningful human control, lifecycle checkpoints, auditability, and defensibility of scientific claims. LEAF therefore shifts AI research governance from retrospective visibility to prospective, risk-proportionate control. We identify boundary conditions, implementation pathways, and an empirical research agenda for testing the framework across disciplines and resource settings. LEAF's distinctive explanatory mechanism is conditional: epistemic materiality escalates oversight, evaluability enables four human capacities, lifecycle checkpoints interrupt error propagation, and retained audit evidence makes consequential decisions answerable.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Digital transformation is reshaping academic work through remote and hybrid arrangements, intensified digital connectivity and the expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI). These developments can support flexibility, autonomy and efficiency, but may also intensify workload, erode work–life boundaries and generate demands associated with continuous adaptation, academic integrity and professional responsibility. Existing evidence is fragmented across technostress, remote and hybrid work, digital readiness and AI-enabled academic work, leaving insufficiently explained how technological change becomes embedded in the organisation and experience of academic work and, through this process, relates to wellbeing. This conceptual paper addresses this gap by developing the Digital Academic Work Reconfiguration and Wellbeing (DAWR-W) Framework. The framework was developed through theory synthesis informed by a structured literature foundation of 40 empirical studies and complementary theoretical research. The synthesis distinguishes the characteristics through which digital transformation reconfigures the organisation, boundaries, demands, relationships and professional content of academic work from the psychosocial mechanisms through which academics experience these changes. The resulting framework identifies seven characteristics of digitally transformed academic work and six psychosocial mechanisms involving resource depletion and replenishment, recovery and psychological detachment, perceived control and autonomy, competence and adaptive capacity, relational connection and psychological safety, and professional meaning and identity. Organisational and institutional conditions shape how digital transformation becomes embedded in academic work, while boundary conditions and feedback processes recognise contextual variation and adaptation over time. The central contribution of the DAWR-W Framework is to position work reconfiguration, rather than technology exposure alone, as the occupational process connecting digital transformation with academic employee wellbeing. In doing so, the framework integrates previously fragmented digital-work phenomena within a common explanatory architecture and locates responsibility for sustainable digital academic work across both individual and institutional levels. It provides an occupation-specific foundation for empirical testing, work-design interventions, and digital and AI governance in higher education.

record.venue: Journal of Economics, Management, Entrepreneurship, and Business (JEMEB)
record.abstract_text: Purpose: This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) driven talent management practices and the performance of agri based enterprises in the Central Region of Cameroon, focusing on the mediating roles of workforce productivity and employee resilience. Research Methodology: A quantitative cross sectional survey design was employed, targeting 250 managers and human resource professionals. Data were collected with a structured questionnaire and analyzed with SPSS and AMOS through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and mediation analysis with 5.000 bootstrap resamples. Results: AI driven talent management was positively and significantly related to enterprise performance (r=0.523, p<0.01). Workforce productivity (β=0.18) and employee resilience (β=0.14) significantly mediated this relationship. Both the total indirect effect (β=0.32, p<0.01) and the direct effect (β=0.29, p<0.01) were significant, indicating partial mediation, with about 52 percent of the total effect transmitted through the two mediators. Conclusions: AI driven talent management enhances the performance of agri based enterprises both directly and indirectly through improved workforce productivity and stronger employee resilience. Enterprises should integrate AI strategically into talent management and support employees through change management. Limitations: The cross sectional design, self reported data, purposive sampling, and focus on a single region limit causal inference and generalizability. Contributions: The study provides empirical evidence from an underresearched African agricultural context and clarifies the mechanisms through which AI driven talent management translates into enterprise performance.

record.abstract_text: As digital technology becomes more deeply embedded in education, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly present in junior high school students' daily learning. This paper explores the "scaffolding" role of GenAI in students' self-regulated learning (SRL) and its possible influence on enhancing academic self-efficacy. Based on Zimmerman's cyclical phase model of SRL and learning scaffolding theory, the study systematically deduces the human-AI interaction process. The analysis suggests that GenAI acts as planning, monitoring, and reflective feedback scaffolds across the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases, effectively addressing the lack of personalized support in traditional autonomous learning. Furthermore, GenAI assistance contributes to the internalization of academic self-efficacy by accumulating direct mastery experiences and alleviating trial-and-error anxiety. Acknowledging the potential risks of cognitive offloading and academic misconduct associated with GenAI dependency, the paper proposes coping strategies such as cultivating students' critical GenAI literacy and implementing dynamic scaffold fading. This research provides theoretical support and practical guidance for educators to optimize GenAI-assisted self-regulated learning environments.

record.abstract_text: Against the backdrop of generative AI emerging as a core strategic asset for major powers, the rhetorical tropes of national security and industrial competitiveness are subject to strategic manipulation by divergent domestic actors. The deregulatory camp within the White House invokes industrial competitiveness to roll back security-focused executive orders; the security faction in Congress expands chip export controls in the name of national defense; state-level authorities counter federal overreach through consumer protection mandates; and Silicon Valley deploys a two-pronged lobbying strategy. Taking the 2023-2026 policy pendulum and BIS chip regulations as its analytical case, this paper demonstrates that domestic contestation spills over globally through transmission channels. This has produced a global AI governance landscape defined by fragmentation, hollowed-out soft law processes, and a three-bloc divide across the U.S., the EU, and China, while the shortening commitment half-life of U.S. policy positions has inflated the costs of multilateral cooperation. The study also identifies limited positive spillover effects. In response, the paper puts forward targeted strategies. The conclusion argues that U.S. internal regulatory divisions constitute a mechanism that externalizes domestic political costs as global governance uncertainty. Understanding this mechanism is a prerequisite for reshaping the multilateral AI order.

record.abstract_text: With AI agents increasingly involved in teamwork, whether AI can substitute human collaboration has become a heated topic in academia. Large-model-driven agents are now capable of participating in team brainstorming, task coordination, and collaborative problem-solving, and knowledge-intensive industries are beginning to form a large number of human-machine hybrid teams. Existing research mostly relies on theoretical reasoning and lacks empirical perceptual data from front-line practitioners. Drawing on a questionnaire survey of 158 employees with cross-industry teamwork experience, this paper explores practitioners' perceptions regarding the substitution of human collaborative behaviors by AI. The results show that AI can only partially substitute procedural and rule-oriented collaborative tasks, whereas social-emotional communication, conflict mediation and value judgment remain irreplaceable human strengths. Position, work experience and AI familiarity jointly shape individual perceptions of the substitution boundary. Most practitioners regard AI as an auxiliary tool rather than a leader of team collaboration. This study provides a practical reference for enterprises applying AI collaboration tools.

record.abstract_text: Background and Aim: Evidence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary science education remains limited. This systematic review examined students’ conceptual understanding and engagement, teachers’ pedagogical strategies and challenges, and students’ critical thinking and scientific inquiry. Materials and Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, ERIC, Scopus, and Lens.org were searched for peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026. Two authors independently screened 187 unique records (Cohen’s κ = .78), identifying 20 eligible studies. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Framework synthesis integrated findings, informed by Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK). Results: Seven studies assessed AI capabilities rather than classroom implementation. Only two compared learning outcomes across conditions; none employed a randomized controlled design. Student perceptions and engagement were generally positive, whereas learning outcomes were mixed. A chatbot supporting self-regulated learning outperformed a rule-based chatbot, but ChatGPT-4o yielded smaller gains than peer collaboration. Teachers reported concerns regarding content accuracy, assessment reliability, and instructional readiness. Generative AI matched or exceeded student performance on structured examinations but demonstrated lower grading reliability than human assessors. Evidence concerning critical thinking was particularly limited. Richer reasoning was reported with dialogue-oriented tools or teacher guidance, whereas answer-seeking use of general-purpose tools was associated with weaker reasoning. Conclusion: Pedagogical structuring was recurrently associated with productive AI use, although causal inference remains limited. A provisional model warrants empirical testing. Priorities include structured tasks, science-specific teacher development, human assessment oversight, explicit AI literacy instruction, school governance, and controlled comparisons of structured and unstructured use across secondary science classrooms.

record.title: Designing Critical Human–AI Learning in Higher Education: The SC-AIM–FAVIC Framework for Analytical and Logical Reasoning

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now routine in university study, yet unstructured use risks cognitive offloading, surface learning, and uncritical acceptance of fluent but unreliable output. This article aimed to develop and specify the Symbiotic Critical Human–AI Learning Model (SC-AIM), operationalised through the five-stage FAVIC framework (Formulation, Augmentation, Verification, Integration, Creation), and to set out the assessment instruments and evaluation design that accompany it. Following the Analysis and Design phases of the ADDIE research-and-development approach, we synthesised recent experimental, meta-analytic, and survey evidence to derive design requirements, translated them into a stage-by-stage instructional specification, built a process-sensitive assessment rubric, and defined a quasi-experimental and qualitative validation plan for Indonesian higher education. The results are the model and its components: an evidence-to-design mapping, the FAVIC stage specification, a three-level process-sensitive rubric, and an evaluation design with hypotheses. Conclusion: SC-AIM offers lecturers a concrete, theory-grounded sequence that places human reasoning before and after AI assistance and makes verification an assessed activity, giving higher education a ready-to-use pedagogical model for developing analytical and logical reasoning in the age of generative AI.

record.abstract_text: The study aimed to check the association of ChatGPT use and critical thinking on academic integrity. The research design is cross-sectional correlational study to collect data from university students aged from 18 to 23 years old. The sample size was 600 students taken via purposive sampling from the University of Gujrat, Pakistan. Standardized psychological scales of ChatGPT usage scale, critical thinking evaluation scale, and academic integrity scales were used. Our findings showed that ChatGPT has no significant effect on academic integrity but has positive effect on critical thinking. While critical thinking has positive effect on academic integrity. It showed that ChatGPT doesn’t directly change cheating behavior, but it can boost critical thinking for students, and that improved critical thinking is what increases academic integrity. Implications of the findings are discussed.

record.title: Neural Mechanisms of Willed Attention Control

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Cueing paradigms are commonly used to study the neural mechanisms of visual spatial attention control. In these paradigms, each trial starts with an external cue, which instructs the subject to pay covert attention to a spatial location in anticipation of an impending stimulus (instructed attention). Recent work has introduced a new type of cue which prompts the subject to spontaneously decide which spatial location to attend (willed attention). We studied the neural mechanisms of willed attention control by analyzing fMRI and EEG data recorded at two institutions (UF and UC Davis) using the same willed attention paradigm. The findings include: (1) both instructional cues and the choice cue activated the DAN, (2) the choice cue additionally activated a frontoparietal decision network consisting of dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), anterior insula (AI), anterior prefrontal cortex (APFC), dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), and inferior parietal lobule (IPL), (3) the decision about where to attend can be decoded in frontoparietal decision network in choice trials but not in instructional trials, and (4) EEG alpha oscillation patterns immediately preceding the choice cue, but not the instructional cues, predicted the postcue direction of attention and the frontoparietal decision network activity. Based on these findings we proposed a model of willed attention control suggesting how the direction of visual spatial attention was decided upon in the absence of external instructions.
